analysis.one_liner: Strengthens workplace harassment and discrimination protections and phases out the lower tipped minimum wage.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 93 House Democrats, never received a vote in any of the five committees it was sent to and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The BE HEARD in the Workplace Act would make it easier to sue over workplace harassment and discrimination: it writes a definition of harassment into federal law, extends protections to independent contractors, interns, and volunteers, applies to employers with even one employee, ends forced arbitration and many nondisclosure clauses in discrimination cases, and removes caps on damages. It also raises the tipped minimum wage in steps until it equals the full federal minimum wage and guarantees workers keep their tips. The bill never got a vote in any committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who face harassment or discrimination — especially tipped restaurant workers, independent contractors, interns, and low-income workers who currently can't afford a lawyer or are forced into private arbitration. All workers gain from a statutory harassment standard that counts a single incident and weighs conduct as a whole, longer deadlines to file claims, and uncapped compensatory damages.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Tipped workers and workers facing harassment

how_it_helps.text: Writes a definition of workplace harassment into federal law and says a single incident can count, with all incidents weighed together rather than one by one — overturning court decisions that dismissed conduct as not 'severe or pervasive' enough.
Phases out the separate tipped minimum wage — starting at $3.60 an hour and rising until it equals the full federal minimum — and guarantees employees the right to keep their tips.
Extends anti-discrimination protections to independent contractors, interns, fellows, volunteers, and trainees, and covers employers with just one employee instead of only those with 15 or more.
Bars employers from forcing workers into predispute arbitration for discrimination claims and prohibits nondisclosure and nondisparagement clauses that silence workers.

Removes the caps on compensatory and punitive damages, extends the deadlines for filing claims, and makes clear that the Religious Freedom Restoration Act cannot be used as a defense to employment discrimination claims.
Creates grant programs for legal help for low-income workers and for state-level worker advocacy systems, plus national training, outreach, and research on harassment through the EEOC.

analysis.who_pays: Employers bear the direct costs: restaurants and other tipped-wage businesses would pay the full minimum wage before tips over several years; all covered employers would face policy, training, and compliance requirements (with fines of up to $1,000 per violation, and at least $5,000 for repeat or willful violations) and greater litigation exposure from easier-to-bring, uncapped claims. Taxpayers would fund the grant programs, national surveys, and EEOC outreach.

drawbacks.text: Covered employers would face new mandates — comprehensive nondiscrimination policies, training, and posting requirements — with fines up to $1,000 per violation and at least $5,000 for repeat or willful violations, a real compliance burden for small businesses.

Removing damage caps and narrowing the proof employers can use raises the cost of defending even weak claims, which critics said would push employers toward settlements regardless of merit — an exposure honest supporters would have to acknowledge.

Phasing out the tip credit raises labor costs sharply for restaurants and other tipped-service businesses, costs that small operators argued could mean higher prices or fewer jobs (a standard objection to tip-credit elimination, based on the wage schedule in the bill text).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers the gains are substantial: a real harassment standard, coverage for contractors and interns, an end to forced arbitration in these cases, and a full minimum wage for tipped workers. The costs fall on employers as compliance burdens, higher tipped wages, and litigation risk, and some of that cost would reach consumers through prices. The bill was broad and ambitious — bundling wage policy, litigation rules, and compliance mandates — which likely made it harder to move, but its core provisions are straightforwardly pro-worker.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in five House committees for more than a year without ever getting a committee vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Representative Katherine Clark introduced the bill on November 17, 2021, with 70 original cosponsors, and it was referred to five committees at once: Education and Labor, Judiciary, House Administration, Oversight and Reform, and Veterans' Affairs.

It was later sent to subcommittees — Oversight and Investigations in November 2021, and the Antitrust and Constitution subcommittees of Judiciary in November 2022 — but no committee ever reported it out.
The bill ended the Congress with 93 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support, having never received a markup or a vote in committee or on the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers — particularly restaurants paying the tipped minimum wage and businesses that rely on forced arbitration and nondisclosure agreements — avoided the new obligations, while workers exposed to harassment and discrimination got no new protections.

sides.party_line_note: All 93 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists to confirm how the parties would have divided.

industries.note: The bill phases out the tipped minimum wage (currently a $2.13 cash wage plus tips) until tipped workers get the full federal minimum, and guarantees they keep their tips. Industry groups have long fought tip-credit elimination because it directly raises their labor costs.

industries.industry: Employers using forced arbitration and NDAs
industries.note: The bill bans predispute arbitration agreements for discrimination claims and restricts nondisclosure and nondisparagement clauses, removing two tools companies use to keep harassment claims quiet and out of court.

All employers with even one employee would face policy, training, and compliance mandates with fines for violations, and easier-to-bring, uncapped claims raise litigation exposure. Some employers would also benefit from clearer statutory standards and federal training materials.
Mandatory nondiscrimination policies and interactive training for employers with 15 or more employees would create demand for training and compliance services.

industries.industry: Legal aid and employment plaintiff lawyers
industries.note: Grant programs for civil legal assistance for low-income workers and state advocacy systems, plus longer filing deadlines and uncapped damages, would expand both funding and demand for worker-side legal representation.
